# Mining the Design Space of Multi-Agent Workflows

Xavier Cadet^($`\alpha`$,\*) Junyan Cheng^($`\alpha`$,\*) Peter
Chin^($`\alpha`$) Kyle Richardson^($`\beta`$)
Affiliation: ^($`\alpha`$)Dartmouth College  ^($`\beta`$)Allen Institute
for AI  
^(\*)Equal contribution.  
{xavier.fjf.cadet,jc.th}@dartmouth.edu kyler@allenai.org  
[Website junyan.ch/apex-paper](https://junyan.ch/apex-paper/)
  [Code github.com/xcadet/apex](https://github.com/xcadet/apex)

###### Abstract

Designing large language model (LLM) multi-agent systems (MAS) still
relies on trial and error and informal “folk wisdom.” Manual studies
test only a few communication structures or topologies (e.g.,
sequential, parallel, shared-memory, or debate), while automated
optimizers discard search trajectories after selecting a task-specific
workflow. We present a two-phase pipeline for mining reproducible design
principles from workflow code and execution traces. We repurpose AFlow’s
MCTS optimizer across six composable operators and 26 deterministically
verified Enigmata tasks, retaining all intermediate rounds to build a
corpus of 28,568 executable workflows. A sandboxed AutoResearch loop
then mines orchestration code and prompt templates under an
$`L_{0}`$-penalized validation objective and tests candidate principles
on held-out searches. Across 300 feature-mining trials, we identify
effects that persist on held-out searches across three levels of
workflow design: workflows beginning with independent solvers and
one-shot aggregation (Star-first) perform worse ($`\Delta=-0.045`$);
persistent shared documents (SharedMemory) outperform debate
($`\Delta=+0.135`$); and prompt specificity and placeholder-based
context routing yield gains comparable to communication-structure
selection ($`\Delta=+0.118`$). More broadly, our pipeline and results
show the feasibility of turning discarded search trajectories into a
statistical testbed for discovering and validating multi-agent workflow
design principles.

¹¹footnotetext: Equal contribution. XC: system implementation & operator
set, large-scale experiments, data analysis, and empirical write-up; JC:
project conception, theoretical framework & instruments, experimental
design, and theoretical write-up.

## I Introduction

Large Language Model (LLM)–based Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) have become a
foundational tool for complex problem solving in many areas such as
software engineering \[[29](#bib.bib30)\], economic forecasting
\[[9](#bib.bib6), [6](#bib.bib9)\], and scientific discovery
\[[21](#bib.bib31), [23](#bib.bib33)\]. In these systems, performance
depends not only on the base LLM, but critically on the workflow
architecture: how agents are connected, how intermediate state is
routed, and how role-specific prompts are structured
\[[19](#bib.bib3)\]. Yet, designing multi-agent workflows remains
largely guided by manual trial-and-error and informal “folk wisdom”
(e.g., “more agents improve accuracy” or “multi-agent debate improves
reasoning”). This raises the question: Can workflow search traces be
used to identify statistically reliable principles for multi-agent
system design?

Fig. 1: Overview of our two-phase pipeline. (1) Sample: for each
verified task bundle $`T`$, an AFlow MCTS search proposes and evaluates
workflows; optimizers keep only the final $`W^{*}`$, whereas we keep
_every_ evaluated node ($`N{=}20`$ rounds $`\times`$ $`K{=}5`$ runs,
failures included). (2) Build a corpus: each of the $`28{,}568`$ entries
is a triplet $`(W,T,\boldsymbol{m})`$, an executable workflow $`W`$
(orchestration code graph.py plus its prompt templates prompt.py), a
task bundle $`T`$, and verified metrics $`\boldsymbol{m}`$ (score,
cost), split into train/val/test at the level of whole searches.
(3) Mine features: a sandboxed AutoResearch loop proposes code and
prompt features $`\boldsymbol{a}=\phi(W)`$ (e.g., the entry operator or
the number of {placeholders}), fits a regressor $`\kappa`$ from
$`(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{t})`$ to $`\boldsymbol{m}`$, and scores
candidates by $`L_{0}`$-penalized validation $`R^{2}`$. (4) Verify
principles: surviving features are tested on held-out searches as score
contrasts $`\Delta`$ between workflows that have vs. lack the feature.

Recent studies have taken initial steps toward quantifying MAS design
choices, examining agent-count scaling \[[34](#bib.bib4)\], load
balancing in compressor-predictor pipelines \[[14](#bib.bib10)\], and
canonical topologies \[[19](#bib.bib3)\]. However, two bottlenecks limit
existing paradigms: (1) *manual empirical studies* evaluate only a
handful of fixed, hand-crafted topologies (typically 3–5 patterns),
leaving composed workflows and sub-topological prompt implementations
unexamined; and (2) *automated workflow optimizers* such as AFlow
\[[33](#bib.bib2)\] and ADAS \[[15](#bib.bib25)\] dynamically search
over code and prompts, but discard over $`95\%`$ of evaluated
architectures to return a single task-specific optimum $`W^{*}`$.

To bridge this gap, we introduce a two-phase empirical pipeline that
transforms complete workflow-search trajectories into a controlled
testbed for discovering design principles
(Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
In the Sampling Phase, we repurpose the MCTS-based AFlow optimizer
\[[33](#bib.bib2)\] to compose six workflow operators: Sequential, Star,
SharedMemory, Debate, StarWithCoordinator, and DebateWithModerator.
Rather than retaining only the final workflow, we collect all $`N=20`$
evaluated workflows from each of $`K=5`$ independent runs per condition.
To limit confounding from external tools, specialized domain knowledge,
and LLM-as-a-judge noise, we evaluate every workflow in a tool-free
setting on 26 deterministically verified reasoning tasks from Enigmata
\[[3](#bib.bib1)\]. This produces a corpus of $`28{,}568`$ executable
workflow–task–performance triplets.

In the Analysis Phase, we run an adapted AutoResearch loop
\[[17](#bib.bib14)\] in a leakage-controlled sandbox with a strict
search-level train/validation/test split. Across 300 trials, it mines
features from orchestration code (graph.py) and role-prompt templates
(prompt.py) under an $`L_{0}`$-regularized validation $`R^{2}`$
objective; we then test 70 candidate contrasts on held-out searches.

Our analysis identifies three effects that persist on held-out searches,
spanning progressively finer levels of workflow specification:
(1) *Entry-Point Topology:* workflows beginning with Star fan-out—in
which parallel workers solve independently before a one-shot aggregator
combines their outputs—perform worse than alternative entry structures
(median $`\Delta=-0.045`$), corroborating [Kim et al.
\[19\]](#bib.bib3)’s finding that uncoordinated agents can amplify
errors; (2) *Communication State:* SharedMemory, in which workers
sequentially update a persistent shared document \[[13](#bib.bib36)\],
outperforms conversational message passing ($`\Delta=+0.135`$); and
(3) *Prompt Structure:* more specific prompt templates and named
placeholders that route context lift validation $`R^{2}`$ from $`0.521`$
with graph features alone to $`0.638`$, with held-out gains
($`\Delta=+0.118`$) comparable to choosing the overall communication or
orchestration topology.

Taken together, our work makes the follow three concrete contributions¹¹

## II Related Work

##### Multi-Agent System Design and Topologies

Designing effective multi-agent LLM workflows has largely relied on
practitioner heuristics \[[27](#bib.bib15), [5](#bib.bib34)\]. While
classical AI established blackboard architectures \[[13](#bib.bib36)\]
where specialist modules read and write to a shared global state, recent
LLM-MAS studies have begun quantifying specific design dimensions:
[Zhang et al. \[34\]](#bib.bib4) and [Qian et al. \[24\]](#bib.bib35)
studied agent-count and collaboration scaling; [He et al.
\[14\]](#bib.bib10) analyzed load balancing in compressor-predictor
pipelines; [Chen et al. \[4\]](#bib.bib28) examined diversity collapse;
[Willis et al. \[28\]](#bib.bib27) studied large agent swarms; and [Kim
et al. \[19\]](#bib.bib3) benchmarked five canonical MAS patterns.
However, these works evaluate a small, fixed set of hand-crafted
topologies and treat prompts as fixed constants. By contrast, we mine
empirical regularities across tens of thousands of dynamically composed
workflows, jointly analyzing macroscopic topologies and sub-topological
prompt structure.

Fig. 2: The six operator primitives $`\mathcal{O}`$ spanning our design
space, drawn for $`n{=}3`$ workers and $`r{=}2`$ rounds. Circles are
worker calls and squares are hub calls (aggregator A, coordinator C,
moderator M); blue edges show which earlier outputs a call reads, purple
edges connect workers to a hub. Sequential chains prompts through one
agent; Star fans out to isolated workers and aggregates once; Debate
lets every worker read all peer proposals before revising; SharedMemory
has workers take turns appending to one persistent document
(blackboard); StarW/Coordinator and DebateW/Moderator add a hub call
after every round. _calls_ counts LLM calls (cost) and _steps_ counts
sequentially dependent calls (latency); with a single round the three
multi-round operators reduce to Star. The optimizer composes operators
in graph.py and writes their prompts in prompt.py
(Fig. [3](#S4.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).

##### Automated Workflow and Prompt Search

Automated search methods have targeted prompt optimization
\[[18](#bib.bib18), [12](#bib.bib19), [1](#bib.bib16)\], graph
connections \[[36](#bib.bib20), [31](#bib.bib21)\], and agent code
evolution \[[32](#bib.bib17)\]. Full-workflow optimizers, including
MCTS-based AFlow \[[33](#bib.bib2)\], MASS \[[35](#bib.bib12)\], ADAS
\[[15](#bib.bib25)\], and supernet routing \[[30](#bib.bib11)\],
iteratively mutate workflow graphs and prompts to maximize accuracy.
Whereas these methods discard intermediate candidates to output a single
workflow $`W^{*}`$, we repurpose MCTS workflow search to harvest
complete search trajectories for population-level analysis.

##### Controlled Reasoning Evaluation

Downstream agentic benchmarks in software engineering
\[[16](#bib.bib29), [29](#bib.bib30)\], API/web interaction
\[[25](#bib.bib23), [10](#bib.bib8)\], and scientific research
\[[2](#bib.bib22)\] conflate multi-agent coordination with domain
knowledge, external tool reliability, and LLM-as-a-judge variance
\[[19](#bib.bib3)\]. To isolate reasoning and coordination, synthetic
benchmarks use verifiable problems in constraint satisfaction
\[[20](#bib.bib13)\], combinatorics \[[22](#bib.bib24)\], and SAT
\[[26](#bib.bib26)\]. We evaluate workflows on Enigmata
\[[3](#bib.bib1)\], leveraging its parametric generators and
deterministic verifiers across difficulty tiers.

## III Formulating Design-Space Mining

Given a collection of executable multi-agent workflows, each evaluated
on a concrete reasoning task $`T`$ (e.g., a bundle of Sudoku instances
checked by a verifier), we ask: _what structural properties of the
workflow designs and prompts reliably predict higher task performance?_
In this section, we introduce our workflow representations and mining
objective
(§ [III-A](#S3.SS1 "III-A Workflow Representation and Mining Objective ‣ III Formulating Design-Space Mining ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
as well as outline the three operational challenges motivating our
pipeline in
§ [III-B](#S3.SS2 "III-B Methodological Challenges in Design-Space Mining ‣ III Formulating Design-Space Mining ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows").

### III-A Workflow Representation and Mining Objective

Following [Kim et al. \[19\]](#bib.bib3) and [Zhang et al.
\[33\]](#bib.bib2), we represent an evaluated agentic system as
$`S=(W,E)`$, pairing an executable workflow $`W\in\mathcal{W}`$ with an
evaluation environment $`E=(T,G)`$. We consider each part in turn.

##### Executable Workflows ($`W`$) and Environment ($`E`$)

A workflow $`W=(\mathcal{N},C,\Omega)`$ is operationalized as an
executable Python program comprising two coupled source files: an
orchestration graph (graph.py) and a prompt module (prompt.py). Here,
$`\mathcal{N}=\{\nu_{1},\nu_{2},\dots\}`$ denotes the LLM-invoking agent
calls, each parameterized by a backbone model $`M_{i}`$, a text prompt
template $`P_{i}`$ (with runtime placeholders such as {problem} or
{worker*outputs}), and temperature $`\tau*{i}`$. The communication
topology $`C`$ and message-routing policy $`\Omega`$ are expressed by
composing multi-agent *operator primitives* from a vocabulary
$`\mathcal{O}`$
(Fig. [2](#S2.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ Multi-Agent System Design and Topologies ‣ II Related Work ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows");
parameters in
Table [VIII](#A3.T8 "TABLE VIII ‣ C-A Operator Set ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"),
§ [C-A](#A3.SS1 "C-A Operator Set ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
The environment $`E=(T,G)`$ pairs a *task bundle* $`T`$ (i.e., *$`M`$
problem instances from a given reasoning task and difficulty tier*) with
a deterministic verifier $`G`$. Executing $`W`$ on $`T`$ yields a
performance vector $`\boldsymbol{m}=G(W,T)\in\mathcal{M}`$, recording
mean verification accuracy ($`\text{score}\in[0,1]`$) and inference cost
(USD).

##### Design-Space Feature Mining

In the _sampling phase_, we collect evaluated workflow triplets
$`\mathcal{D}=\{(W_{i},T_{i},\boldsymbol{m}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}`$.
Because each $`W_{i}`$ is raw source code, in the _analysis phase_ we
search for a programmatic feature extractor
$`\phi:\mathcal{W}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}`$ that parses graph.py and prompt.py
into an interpretable feature vector $`\boldsymbol{a}=\phi(W)`$ (e.g.,
operator counts, entry-point topology, or prompt template length and
placeholder count), alongside task descriptors
$`\boldsymbol{t}=\psi(T)`$ and a regressor $`\kappa`$. Optimizing
$`(\phi,\psi,\kappa)\in\mathbf{H}`$ on train/validation splits yields
candidate features $`\mathcal{H}\subset\mathbf{H}`$. Each candidate is
then verified on held-out test searches by splitting the workflows of
every puzzle into two _arms_, as in an A/B test, a _high arm_ in which
the feature is present (or above the per-puzzle median) and a _low arm_
in which it is absent (or at/below the median), and estimating the
per-puzzle contrast
$`\Delta=\mathbb{E}[\text{score}\mid\text{high arm}]-\mathbb{E}[\text{score}\mid\text{low arm}]`$
(§ [V-B](#S5.SS2 "V-B Mining and Verifying Design Principles ‣ V Empirical Analysis ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).

### III-B Methodological Challenges in Design-Space Mining

Extracting reliable empirical principles from observational workflow
data requires overcoming three operational challenges (summarized in
Table [II](#A1.T2 "TABLE II ‣ Appendix A Methodological Formalization and Statistical Estimands ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
and formalized in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Methodological Formalization and Statistical Estimands ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")):

##### Challenge 1: Design-Space Coverage vs. Implementation Competence

Mining principles requires a sample that both _covers_ many distinct
designs and consists of _competent_ implementations. The naive route to
coverage, generating workflow programs from scratch (e.g., prompting an
LLM to write arbitrary orchestration code and prompts without
constraints), fails the second requirement: most candidates break with
syntax errors or degenerate prompts, burying topological effects under
implementation noise. Conversely, keeping only an optimizer’s final
argmax workflow $`W^{*}`$ discards the negative and intermediate
examples needed to estimate contrasts. We therefore repurpose the
MCTS-based AFlow optimizer
(§ [IV-A](#S4.SS1 "IV-A Sampling Phase: Full-Trace Workflow Search via AFlow ‣ IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"))
over a structured 6-operator vocabulary $`\mathcal{O}`$ and retain _all_
$`N=20`$ intermediate workflows per search under a consistent LLM
optimizer policy.

##### Challenge 2: Domain, Tool, and Grading Confounds

On downstream benchmarks such as software engineering or web navigation,
accuracy is conflated with domain knowledge, external tool reliability,
and LLM-as-a-judge grading noise \[[19](#bib.bib3)\]. To isolate
multi-agent coordination and prompt structure, we evaluate workflows in
a tool-free setting using Enigmata
(§ [IV-B](#S4.SS2 "IV-B Sampling Phase: Controlled Reasoning Evaluation via Enigmata ‣ IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
where tasks are self-contained abstract reasoning puzzles scored by
exact, deterministic rule-based verifiers on fixed instance bundles.

##### Challenge 3: High-Dimensional Feature Overfitting and Leakage

Because infinitely many features can be parsed from graph.py and
prompt.py, manual feature selection is narrow, whereas unconstrained
search can overfit or exploit dataset artifacts (such as MCTS round
indices or within-search correlation). We address this via an
$`L_{0}`$-regularized validation objective
(§ [IV-C](#S4.SS3 "IV-C Analysis Phase: Sandboxed Feature Mining via AutoResearch ‣ IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"))
inside a strict sandbox, partitioning $`\mathcal{D}`$ into train,
validation, and test splits at the _AFlow search level_ and stripping
all search/round identifiers from workflow files.

## IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases

Fig. 3: Composing operators in graph.py. A Star workflow (three workers,
one aggregator) drafts a Sudoku solution; graph.py then forwards the
_original_ puzzle together with the draft into a one-step Sequential
validator. Every call’s prompt template lives in prompt.py, with
placeholders such as {problem} and {worker_outputs} filled at run time.
Features such as the entry operator, chain length, and placeholder
counts are parsed from exactly these two files.

Fig. 4: Full-Trace AFlow Search. Macro-mean raw score per MCTS round by
puzzle category ($`1{,}701`$ searches, $`26`$ puzzles; $`95\%`$
bootstrap CIs); retaining all 20 rounds captures a wide performance
trajectory.

Fig. 5: AutoResearch Feature-Mining Trace. Validation $`R^{2}`$ (left
axis) and active feature count $`\|\phi\|_{0}`$ (right axis) over
iterations; the $`L_{0}`$-penalized objective improves fit while pruning
redundant features.

Our pipeline operates in two stages: a sampling phase that pairs
full-trace AFlow workflow search
(§ [IV-A](#S4.SS1 "IV-A Sampling Phase: Full-Trace Workflow Search via AFlow ‣ IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"))
with deterministic Enigmata evaluation
(§ [IV-B](#S4.SS2 "IV-B Sampling Phase: Controlled Reasoning Evaluation via Enigmata ‣ IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
followed by an analysis phase that mines workflow code and prompt
features via a sandboxed AutoResearch loop
(§ [IV-C](#S4.SS3 "IV-C Analysis Phase: Sandboxed Feature Mining via AutoResearch ‣ IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).

### IV-A Sampling Phase: Full-Trace Workflow Search via AFlow

In AFlow \[[33](#bib.bib2)\], each workflow $`W`$ is represented as an
executable Python class in graph.py accompanied by role-specific hard
text prompt templates in prompt.py (no soft prompts or gradient
updates). Given a task bundle $`T`$, AFlow searches over workflows
across $`N=20`$ MCTS rounds: (i) *Selection:* A parent workflow is
sampled from the top-$`k`$ ($`k=4`$) evaluated workflows using a mixed
uniform/softmax distribution ($`\lambda=0.2`$ uniform weight,
temperature $`\alpha=0.4`$;
Eq. [4](#A3.E4 "In C-B Parent Selection Policy ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
in
§ [C-B](#A3.SS2 "C-B Parent Selection Policy ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"))
to prevent premature collapse; (ii) *Expansion:* An LLM optimizer (fixed
to GPT-5.4 at temperature $`0`$) inspects the parent’s code and score
history and proposes an edit that adds, removes, or rechains operators
in graph.py and refines role prompts in prompt.py
(§ [D-D](#A4.SS4 "D-D Prompts ‣ Appendix D Analysis Phase Methodology ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"));
(iii) *Evaluation:* The child workflow is executed on the $`M=20`$
instances in $`T`$; and (iv) *Backpropagation:* Scores and costs are
recorded in the search tree. Steps (i)–(iv) are the unmodified AFlow
loop; we change three things
(§ [C-C](#A3.SS3 "C-C AFlow Integration ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
First, the operator registry is replaced by our six primitives
(Fig. [2](#S2.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ Multi-Agent System Design and Topologies ‣ II Related Work ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
so every proposed edit is a composition of known topologies. Second,
evaluation targets fixed Enigmata bundles with deterministic verifiers
(§ [IV-B](#S4.SS2 "IV-B Sampling Phase: Controlled Reasoning Evaluation via Enigmata ‣ IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
Third, unlike point optimization that returns only $`W^{*}`$, we retain
_all_ $`N=20`$ workflows per trace across $`K=5`$ independent runs per
condition, capturing both successful and failed designs below the
best-so-far envelope
(Fig. [5](#S4.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows");
single tree in
Fig. [11](#A8.F11 "Fig. 11 ‣ Appendix H Trace Examples ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"),
§ [H](#A8 "Appendix H Trace Examples ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).

##### Composable Operator Primitives and Roles

To span established coordination patterns while permitting multi-stage
compositions, we equip the search space with six operator primitives
$`\mathcal{O}`$
(Fig. [2](#S2.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ Multi-Agent System Design and Topologies ‣ II Related Work ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"),
Table [VIII](#A3.T8 "TABLE VIII ‣ C-A Operator Set ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows");
§ [C-A](#A3.SS1 "C-A Operator Set ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
synthesized from recent MAS surveys \[[19](#bib.bib3), [35](#bib.bib12),
[30](#bib.bib11), [5](#bib.bib34)\]: single-agent linear chaining
(Sequential), isolated parallel fan-out followed by one-shot aggregation
(Star), blackboard-style sequential writing to a persistent shared
document (SharedMemory; [13](#bib.bib36)), all-to-all peer proposal
exchange (Debate), and hub-and-spoke or moderated multi-round variants
(StarWithCoordinator, DebateWithModerator). An _operation_ in graph.py
is an asynchronous call to one operator primitive with optimizer-chosen
parameters: $`n\in[1,10]`$ workers, $`r\in[1,5]`$ _rounds_, and custom
prompts in prompt.py. A round is one complete pass of the operator’s
communication pattern, e.g., every SharedMemory worker reads the
document once and appends to it, or every Debate worker reads its peers’
proposals once and revises, and an operator with $`r>1`$ repeats this
pass $`r`$ times, each pass conditioned on the previous one
(Fig. [2](#S2.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ Multi-Agent System Design and Topologies ‣ II Related Work ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
is drawn for $`r{=}2`$); these operator rounds are distinct from the
$`N{=}20`$ MCTS _search_ rounds above. Operations can be chained
sequentially or conditionally, with the outputs of one operator (and the
original problem) forwarded into the prompts of the next (e.g.,
$`\textsc{Star}\to\textsc{Sequential}`$ in
Fig. [3](#S4.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows");
the most common chains are listed in
Table [XII](#A5.T12 "TABLE XII ‣ Test-split cluster support ‣ E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
Each operator uses up to two LLM roles (a _worker_ and an
_aggregator/coordinator/moderator_) drawn from
$`\{\texttt{GPT-5.4-mini},\texttt{GPT-5.4-nano}\}`$, with at most $`20`$
LLM calls per workflow execution
(§ [B](#A2 "Appendix B Experiment Details and Hyperparameters ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).

### IV-B Sampling Phase: Controlled Reasoning Evaluation via Enigmata

All agents operate in a _pure-reasoning, tool-free setting_ (no code
interpreters or search tools), so collaboration acts only through task
decomposition, diverse candidate generation, peer verification, and
shared state tracking. We select all $`30`$ tasks in Enigmata
\[[3](#bib.bib1)\] (_Crypto, Arithmetic, Logic, Grid, Graph, Search, and
Sequential_ categories) with programmatic generators and deterministic
rule-based verifiers (exact match $`\in\{0,1\}`$), yielding $`87`$
(puzzle, difficulty) bundles across {Easy, Medium, Hard}. For each
bundle $`T`$, we deterministically generate $`M=20`$ instances and reuse
this fixed set across all $`K=5`$ searches and $`N=20`$ rounds within
that bundle so score differences reflect workflow structure rather than
instance sampling noise
(§ [C-D](#A3.SS4 "C-D Enigmata Specification ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
Filtering $`1{,}031`$ syntax-invalid workflows ($`3.0\%`$) and excluding
$`4`$ sliding-tile puzzles where all single-agent baselines and
workflows scored $`0.00`$
(§ [C-E](#A3.SS5 "C-E Filtered Puzzles and Failure Modes ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"))
yields $`28{,}568`$ executable workflows across $`26`$ puzzles.

### IV-C Analysis Phase: Sandboxed Feature Mining via AutoResearch

To extract design principles from graph.py and prompt.py, we adapt
AutoResearch \[[17](#bib.bib14)\] as an automated feature-mining loop.
At each iteration, an LLM agent edits a feature-extraction and
regression script (train.py) that parses workflow source files into
features $`\phi(W)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}`$, joins them with task descriptors
$`\psi(T)`$, and fits per-puzzle regressors $`\kappa`$ on
$`D_{\text{train}}`$. To enforce parsimony and mitigate overfitting,
each candidate is scored on the held-out validation split
$`D_{\text{val}}`$ via an $`L_{0}`$-regularized validation objective
$`\mathcal{F}(\phi,\psi,\kappa)`$ defined as:

|     |                                                |                                                                                                          |     |     |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(\phi,\psi,\kappa)`$ | $`\displaystyle=R^{2}_{D_{\mathrm{val}}}(\boldsymbol{m},\widehat{\boldsymbol{m}})-\lambda\|\phi\|_{0},`$ |     | (1) |
|     | $`\displaystyle\widehat{\boldsymbol{m}}`$      | $`\displaystyle=\kappa\bigl(\phi(W),\psi(T)\bigr).`$                                                     |     |     |

where $`\|\phi\|_{0}=d`$ penalizes active feature count
(Fig. [5](#S4.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows");
multi-run comparison in
Fig. [7](#A4.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ Appendix D Analysis Phase Methodology ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).

##### Search-Level Splitting and Sandbox Isolation

Because workflows within the same MCTS trace are evolutionary
descendants, we partition the corpus into training ($`69.4\%`$),
validation ($`15.0\%`$), and held-out test ($`15.6\%`$) splits strictly
at the _AFlow search level_
(Table [IX](#A5.T9 "TABLE IX ‣ E-A Statistics ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows");
§ [D-A](#A4.SS1.SSS0.Px1 "Train / val / test split provenance ‣ D-A Feature Engineering and Models ‣ Appendix D Analysis Phase Methodology ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
The feature-mining loop operates in a read-only sandbox that strips all
search hashes, MCTS round indices, and file paths from workflow sources,
forbids target-derived encodings, and physically isolates
$`D_{\text{test}}`$ for final verification
(§ [D-C](#A4.SS3 "D-C Caveats and Mitigated Failure Modes ‣ Appendix D Analysis Phase Methodology ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).

### V-A Workflow Corpus and Coverage

Our corpus comprises $`28{,}568`$ executable multi-agent workflows
across $`26`$ Enigmata puzzles ($`1{,}701`$ completed AFlow search
traces out of $`1{,}740`$ grid cells;
Tables [IX](#A5.T9 "TABLE IX ‣ E-A Statistics ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
and
[XIII](#A5.T13 "TABLE XIII ‣ Test-split cluster support ‣ E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"),
§ [E](#A5 "Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
evaluated on 20-instance bundles at $`\$0.0064`$ per puzzle instance
($`\sim\$4{,}454`$ total compute;
Table [X](#A5.T10 "TABLE X ‣ Test-split cluster support ‣ E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"),
§ [G](#A7 "Appendix G Computational Cost Analysis ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
Workflows exercise all six operators individually and in chains:
Sequential ($`47.2\%`$), Star ($`44.5\%`$), Debate ($`22.3\%`$),
SharedMemory ($`20.8\%`$), DebateWithModerator ($`11.8\%`$), and
StarWithCoordinator ($`8.8\%`$;
Tables [XI](#A5.T11 "TABLE XI ‣ Test-split cluster support ‣ E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")–[XII](#A5.T12 "TABLE XII ‣ Test-split cluster support ‣ E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).

##### Single-Agent Baselines, Coverage, and Sufficiency

Against one-shot evaluations of the single-agent backbones (GPT-5.4,
GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-5.4-nano) on the identical puzzle bundles
(Table [XIV](#A5.T14 "TABLE XIV ‣ Test-split cluster support ‣ E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"),
§ [F](#A6 "Appendix F Single-Backbone Baseline Performance ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
multi-agent workflows using only mini/nano workers substantially
outperform even the stronger GPT-5.4 baseline on tasks requiring
iterative constraint propagation, lifting accuracy from
$`0.100\to 0.891`$ (mean) and $`1.000`$ (max) on
NaturalLanguageNavigation, $`0.033\to 0.359`$ on MagicSquare, and
$`0.467\to 0.849`$ on StackPermutation. Full MCTS traces capture
workflows spanning three orders of magnitude in cost ($`\$0.01`$ to
$`>\$3.00`$ per bundle) and the full $`[0,1]`$ accuracy range
(Fig. [8](#A5.F8 "Fig. 8 ‣ E-A Statistics ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
while the running cell mean converges within a $`0.02`$ tolerance well
before the full budget ($`N_{\text{cfg}}=59`$ searches per puzzle;
Fig. [9](#A5.F9 "Fig. 9 ‣ E-A Statistics ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"),
Fig. [10](#A5.F10 "Fig. 10 ‣ E-A Statistics ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).

### V-B Mining and Verifying Design Principles

##### Candidate Pool and Predictability Gating

We executed $`10`$ main AutoResearch runs (graph.py only vs. graph.py
$`+`$ prompt.py;
Fig. [7](#A4.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ Appendix D Analysis Phase Methodology ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
totaling $`300`$ automated feature-engineering trials
(§ [E-C](#A5.SS3 "E-C Candidate Hypothesis Set ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
While graph.py-only feature sets plateaued at validation $`R^{2}=0.521`$
($`8`$ features), jointly parsing prompt.py lifted validation $`R^{2}`$
to $`0.638`$ ($`27`$ features), yielding $`70`$ candidate binarized
contrasts. Within each puzzle, workflows are split into high and low
arms as defined in
§ [III-A](#S3.SS1 "III-A Workflow Representation and Mining Objective ‣ III Formulating Design-Space Mining ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
($`\geq 20`$ workflows per arm) to estimate $`\Delta`$ with $`95\%`$
cluster-robust Wald CIs clustered by AFlow search ID
(§ [E-B](#A5.SS2 "E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
To avoid diluting contrasts with floor/ceiling tasks, a pre-test
_predictability gate_ admits a puzzle iff a LightGBM surrogate trained
on $`D_{\text{train}}`$ achieves validation $`R^{2}>0.05`$ and Spearman
$`\rho>0.30`$ on $`D_{\text{val}}`$
(§ [I](#A9 "Appendix I Gate Calibration ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
Calibrated against a permutation null ($`R^{2}_{p95}\leq-0.06`$,
$`\rho_{p95}\leq 0.23`$;
Fig. [12](#A9.F12 "Fig. 12 ‣ Appendix I Gate Calibration ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
this gate admits $`13`$ predictable puzzles prior to accessing
$`D_{\text{test}}`$
(Fig. [6](#S5.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ V Empirical Analysis ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"),
Table [I](#S5.T1 "TABLE I ‣ V Empirical Analysis ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows");
Table [XV](#A5.T15 "TABLE XV ‣ E-C Candidate Hypothesis Set ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")):

##### Principle 1 (RQ1, Entry-Point Topology): Star-first fan-out degrades reasoning

When a workflow begins with an isolated Star operator (parallel workers
without lateral communication followed by one-shot aggregation),
accuracy drops relative to alternative entry topologies on $`7/13`$
train puzzles ($`\text{median }\Delta=-0.036`$,
$`p_{\mathrm{W}}=.008`$), with $`0/13`$ strictly positive cells
(Fig. [6](#S5.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ V Empirical Analysis ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
left;
Table [V](#A2.T5 "TABLE V ‣ B-B1 Per-Puzzle Breakdowns of Mined Principles ‣ B-B Analysis Phase ‣ Appendix B Experiment Details and Hyperparameters ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
This negative effect persists on the held-out test split
($`\text{median }\Delta=-0.045`$, $`p_{\mathrm{W}}=.038`$, $`9/10`$
conditional sign replication), corroborating [Kim et al.
\[19\]](#bib.bib3): uncoordinated parallel fan-out amplifies reasoning
errors that an aggregator must then reconcile without peer verification.

##### Principle 2 (RQ2, Communication State): SharedMemory outperforms conversational dialogue

Whereas LLM frameworks default to conversational message passing
(Debate), workflows using blackboard-style SharedMemory
\[[13](#bib.bib36)\], in which agents sequentially read and append to a
persistent written document, outperform workflows without it on
$`10/13`$ train puzzles ($`\text{median }\Delta=+0.072`$,
$`p_{\mathrm{W}}=.002`$) and $`6/10`$ test puzzles
($`\text{median }\Delta=+0.135`$, $`p_{\mathrm{W}}=.011`$, $`9/10`$ sign
agreement;
Fig. [6](#S5.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ V Empirical Analysis ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
middle,
Table [VI](#A2.T6 "TABLE VI ‣ B-B1 Per-Puzzle Breakdowns of Mined Principles ‣ B-B Analysis Phase ‣ Appendix B Experiment Details and Hyperparameters ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
achieving the highest corpus-wide mean accuracy of all six operators
($`0.23`$ vs. $`0.18`$ for Debate and $`0.16`$ for Star;
Table [XI](#A5.T11 "TABLE XI ‣ Test-split cluster support ‣ E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
showing that persistent written state mitigates “lossy communication” in
multi-round dialogue \[[19](#bib.bib3)\].

##### Principle 3 (RQ3, Sub-Topological Prompt Structure): prompt specificity and placeholder routing predict accuracy

Below the categorical topology grain, workflows with above-median prompt
template character length (mean chars in prompt.py) achieve strictly
positive accuracy gains on $`11/13`$ train
($`\text{median }\Delta=+0.073`$, $`p_{\mathrm{W}}=.002`$) and $`6/13`$
test puzzles ($`\text{median }\Delta=+0.118`$, $`p_{\mathrm{W}}=.002`$,
$`13/13`$ sign agreement;
Fig. [6](#S5.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ V Empirical Analysis ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
right,
Table [VII](#A2.T7 "TABLE VII ‣ B-B1 Per-Puzzle Breakdowns of Mined Principles ‣ B-B Analysis Phase ‣ Appendix B Experiment Details and Hyperparameters ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
Similarly, the count of {name} placeholders (\#placeh.) replicates this
positive effect on $`9/13`$ train ($`\text{median }\Delta=+0.102`$) and
$`7/13`$ test puzzles ($`\text{median }\Delta=+0.059`$, $`11/13`$ sign
agreement). We do not claim character length is causal in isolation;
rather, sub-topological prompt specification and context routing carry
effect sizes ($`\Delta\approx+0.06\text{ to }+0.12`$) on par with
macro-topology selection, which is why prompt.py features lift
validation $`R^{2}`$ from $`0.521`$ to $`0.638`$
(Fig. [7](#A4.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ Appendix D Analysis Phase Methodology ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).

##### Out-of-Sample Verification and Test Precision

Across all seven variants in
Table [I](#S5.T1 "TABLE I ‣ V Empirical Analysis ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"),
two-sided Wilcoxon tests ($`p_{\mathrm{W}}<0.05`$), binomial
sign-agreement tests ($`p_{\mathrm{B}}^{\cap}\leq.001`$), and
conditional test-verification tests
($`p_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{tr}}\leq.035`$) confirm directional
reproducibility on $`D_{\text{test}}`$. Median effect sizes hold on
test, but fewer puzzles clear strict 95% cluster-Wald CIs
($`k_{+}/k_{-}`$) than on train (e.g., $`4/12`$ vs. $`7/13`$ for
Star-first; $`6/10`$ vs. $`10/13`$ for SharedMemory) because the
$`15.6\%`$ test split has fewer search clusters ($`G\in[4,14]`$ vs.
$`[19,47]`$;
§ [E-B](#A5.SS2 "E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")):
the findings are directionally robust, with finite-sample uncertainty on
task-specific magnitudes.

## VI Discussion and Future Directions

##### Full-Trace Mining vs. Point Optimization

Automated workflow search and empirical design-space science are
complementary: the non-argmax rounds that search discards provide
exactly the negative and intermediate comparisons needed to explain why
designs fail and which edits help. Full traces also expose accuracy-cost
trade-offs: SharedMemory costs more than Debate or Star (\$0.25 vs.
\$0.13;
Table [XI](#A5.T11 "TABLE XI ‣ Test-split cluster support ‣ E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"))
as the shared document grows, yet its persistent written state avoids
the information loss of multi-round dialogue and yields the highest mean
accuracy in the corpus.

##### Beyond Topology-Only Benchmarks

Macro-topology alone (graph.py) explains only part of workflow variance
($`R^{2}=0.521`$); jointly mining sub-topological prompt structure
(prompt.py) lifts out-of-sample predictive power to $`R^{2}=0.638`$
(§ [V-B](#S5.SS2 "V-B Mining and Verifying Design Principles ‣ V Empirical Analysis ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
Topology benchmarks should therefore report and control for prompt
template richness and placeholder routing rather than treating prompts
as fixed constants: an ostensibly superior communication graph can be
bottlenecked by underspecified role instructions or missing context
placeholders.

##### Operator Evolution and Tool-Rich Domains

Feeding mined regularities back into the operator registry could guide
the synthesis of new operator primitives \[[23](#bib.bib33),
[8](#bib.bib5)\] or prune suboptimal entry-point patterns (such as
uncoordinated Star-first fan-out) from the optimizer’s search prior, and
extending the pipeline to tool-rich domains such as coding
\[[16](#bib.bib29)\], games \[[11](#bib.bib32)\], and social simulations
\[[7](#bib.bib7)\] will test how topological and prompt principles
interact with external tool use and environment feedback.

## VII Conclusion

We presented an end-to-end pipeline that moves multi-agent LLM workflow
design from manual “folk wisdom” toward systematic statistical mining of
design principles. Full-trace AFlow search over 26 deterministically
verified Enigmata tasks yielded $`28{,}568`$ executable workflows, and a
sandboxed, search-level-split AutoResearch loop over 300 trials surfaced
out-of-sample verified principles at three granularities: Star-first
fan-out degrades accuracy, blackboard-style SharedMemory outperforms
conversational debate, and prompt template specificity and placeholder
routing matter as much as macroscopic topology. We release the workflow
corpus, evaluation harness, and sandboxed analysis pipeline for
reproducible empirical research on multi-agent systems.

## Limitations

To isolate multi-agent coordination and prompt structure from external
confounds, our experiments focus on tool-free, deterministically
verified reasoning tasks from Enigmata and evaluate workflows within a
single model family (GPT-5.4 as the MCTS optimizer and {GPT-5.4-mini,
GPT-5.4-nano} as worker and aggregator backbones;
§ [B](#A2 "Appendix B Experiment Details and Hyperparameters ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
While this controlled setup eliminates grading noise and API variance
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Methodological Formalization and Statistical Estimands ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
extending our pipeline to open-weight model families, alternative
workflow search algorithms, and tool-interactive domains (such as
repository-level coding or web navigation) is a natural direction for
future work. Finally, because our corpus harvests trajectories generated
along MCTS optimization runs, the mined principles reflect structural
regularities within the space of executable workflows explored by the
optimizer rather than unconstrained random code generation.

## Appendix A Methodological Formalization and Statistical Estimands

As introduced in
§ [III](#S3 "III Formulating Design-Space Mining ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"),
our pipeline mines empirical design principles from observational
workflow trajectories
$`\mathcal{D}=\{(W_{i},T_{i},\boldsymbol{m}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}`$.
Here we formalize the statistical estimands recovered by our approach
and clarify how each stage (AFlow traversal, Enigmata verification, and
search-level sandboxed AutoResearch) addresses key threats to validity
when learning from non-randomized workflow corpora;
Table [II](#A1.T2 "TABLE II ‣ Appendix A Methodological Formalization and Statistical Estimands ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
maps each challenge to the pipeline component that addresses it.

[TABLE]

TABLE II: Core methodological challenges in empirical MAS design-space
mining and corresponding pipeline components. Each stage of the pipeline
addresses a specific operational threat to extracting reproducible
design principles.

### A-A Implementation Variance and Policy-Conditioned Sampling

When mapping a raw workflow $`W`$ (consisting of graph.py and prompt.py)
into an interpretable feature vector $`\boldsymbol{a}=\phi(W)`$,
microscopic implementation details $`\theta_{s}\in\Theta_{s}`$ (such as
exact phrasing choices or variable names not captured by $`\phi`$)
remain unmodeled. Marginalizing over the distribution of implementation
details under a sampling policy $`\mathcal{L}`$, the expected
performance of workflows with feature profile $`\boldsymbol{a}`$ on task
$`\boldsymbol{t}`$ is:

[TABLE]

##### Why MCTS Trajectory Harvesting Beats Naive Random Code Sampling

If $`\mathcal{L}`$ were a uniform random code-and-string generator over
$`\Theta_{s}`$, the vast majority of sampled workflows would contain
syntax errors or incoherent prompts, causing extreme variance in
$`\theta_{s}`$ to swamp structural differences in $`\boldsymbol{a}`$.
Conversely, retaining only the final argmax $`W^{*}`$ from an optimizer
collapses support onto a single point per search. By harvesting all
$`N=20`$ MCTS rounds generated under a fixed LLM optimizer (GPT-5.4 at
temperature $`0`$) with a mixed uniform/softmax parent-selection policy
($`\lambda=0.2`$;
Eq. [4](#A3.E4 "In C-B Parent Selection Policy ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
AFlow restricts $`\Theta_{s}`$ to syntactically valid, competently
prompted implementations while preserving broad variation across
operators and prompt templates. Importantly, as noted in our
Limitations, $`\mu_{\mathcal{L}}(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{t})`$
represents a _policy-conditioned observational estimand_ relative to the
foundation model’s capability frontier rather than an unconditioned
interventional effect.

### A-B Evaluation Variance and Fixed-Bundle Verification

Let $`G(W,T)`$ denote the observed evaluation score of workflow $`W`$ on
task bundle $`T=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{M}\}`$. In open-ended benchmarks that
rely on external tool APIs, web state, or LLM-as-a-judge grading, the
observed score decomposes as:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\widehat{\boldsymbol{m}}(W,T)=\mu_{\text{reasoning}}(W,T)+\xi_{\text{domain/tool}}+\epsilon_{\text{judge}}
``` |  | (3) |

where $`\xi_{\text{domain/tool}}`$ reflects external API or
domain-knowledge bottlenecks and $`\epsilon_{\text{judge}}`$ represents
grading noise.

##### Deterministic Verification on Reused Bundles (Enigmata)

Evaluating tool-free workflows on Enigmata \[[3](#bib.bib1)\] eliminates
subjective judge variance ($`\epsilon_{\text{judge}}=0`$) because every
puzzle instance is scored by an exact, deterministic rule-based
verifier. Furthermore, because the same fixed bundle of $`M=20`$
deterministically generated instances is reused across all $`K=5`$
searches and $`N=20`$ MCTS rounds within each (puzzle, difficulty) cell
(§ [C-D](#A3.SS4 "C-D Enigmata Specification ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
instance-sampling variance between workflows compared within the same
cell cancels out in paired per-puzzle contrasts
$`\Delta=\mathbb{E}[\text{score}\mid\text{high arm}]-\mathbb{E}[\text{score}\mid\text{low arm}]`$.

### A-C Overfitting, Trajectory Leakage, and Out-of-Sample Verification

Let $`S(\phi)\in\{0,1\}`$ denote the indicator that a candidate feature
extractor $`\phi\in\mathbf{H}`$ is selected during feature mining. Two
forms of overfitting threaten automated feature discovery over workflow
code: (1) *within-search trajectory leakage*, where correlated MCTS
rounds from the same search straddle training and evaluation splits; and
(2) *test-set selection leakage*, where feature selection $`S(\phi)`$
conditions on held-out test outcomes $`\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{test}}`$.

##### Search-Level Splitting and Pre-Specified Test Verification

Our analysis phase prevents both failure modes structurally. First,
partitioning $`\mathcal{D}`$ into $`D_{\text{train}}`$,
$`D_{\text{val}}`$, and $`D_{\text{test}}`$ at the *AFlow search level*
guarantees that all $`N=20`$ rounds of any search trajectory reside in a
single split. Second, the AutoResearch loop evaluates the
$`L_{0}`$-penalized objective $`\mathcal{F}(\phi,\psi,\kappa)`$
(Eq. [1](#S4.E1 "In IV-C Analysis Phase: Sandboxed Feature Mining via AutoResearch ‣ IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"))
exclusively on $`D_{\text{val}}`$ inside an isolated sandbox with no
access to $`D_{\text{test}}`$ or row/round identifiers. Because both the
candidate features $`\phi`$ and the hypothesized contrast directions are
fixed prior to accessing $`D_{\text{test}}`$, the selection mechanism
satisfies conditional independence
$`S(\phi)\perp\!\!\!\perp\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{test}}\mid\boldsymbol{a}`$,
ensuring that test-split contrasts provide a valid, uncontaminated
out-of-sample replication check.

| Exploration/Exploitation weight ($`\lambda`$) | 0.2 |
| Top-$`k`$ score-based selection | 4 |
| Score influence factor $`\lambda`$ | 0.4 |
| Predictability gating |  |
| $`R^{2}`$ threshold | $`0.05`$ |
| $`\rho`$ threshold | $`0.30`$ |
| Min entry per cell | $`20`$ |
| Model | LightGBM |
| Learning rate | $`0.05`$ |
| Number of leaves | $`31`$ |

TABLE III: Hyper-parameters

##### Model selection

The Optimizer role, which proposes structural workflow modifications
during AFlow search, is fixed to GPT-5.4 in order to maintain a single,
stationary generative policy across the corpus (cf.
§ [A](#A1 "Appendix A Methodological Formalization and Statistical Estimands ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
The Worker and Aggregator roles are drawn from
$`\{\text{GPT-5.4-mini},\text{GPT-5.4-nano}\}`$, providing a controlled
$`2\times 2`$ contrast between worker and aggregator capability while
keeping the per-search call budget tractable.

##### Workflow constraints

Each generated workflow is capped at $`20`$ atomic LLM calls, which
bounds the per-evaluation cost while still admitting compositions of
multiple operators
(§[C-A](#A3.SS1 "C-A Operator Set ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
Because each workflow is evaluated on the full $`20`$-instance bundle,
this caps the per-search call budget at $`20\times 20=400`$ atomic calls
per round and at most $`8{,}000`$ calls for an entire AFlow search
trace. The operator set comprises the six primitives listed in
Table [VIII](#A3.T8 "TABLE VIII ‣ C-A Operator Set ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows").

##### AFlow search

Each (puzzle, bundle, model) cell is searched $`K=5`$ times for $`N=20`$
MCTS rounds. The selection mixture
(Eq. [4](#A3.E4 "In C-B Parent Selection Policy ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"))
uses $`\lambda=0.2`$ to balance uniform exploration against
score-weighted exploitation, with score temperature $`\alpha=0.4`$ and a
top-$`k`$ pool of size $`k=4`$.

##### Predictability gate

The LightGBM surrogate (200 trees, learning rate $`0.05`$, $`31`$
leaves, min_child_samples $`=10`$, fixed seed) used for the
predictability gate admits a puzzle if $`R^{2}>0.05`$ *and* Spearman
$`\rho>0.30`$ on its validation rows; the calibration of these
thresholds against a permutation null is detailed in
§[I](#A9 "Appendix I Gate Calibration ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows").
The minimum cell occupancy of $`20`$ workflows in either arm is enforced
for every per-puzzle binarized contrast.

|--------------|-------------------------|
| GPT-5.4      | gpt-5.4-2026-03-05      |
| GPT-5.4-mini | gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17 |
| GPT-5.4-nano | gpt-5.4-nano-2026-03-17 |

### B-A Enigmata puzzles

We selected a subset of the Enigmata puzzles, namely we focused on 30
puzzles for which the code-base provided both generator and verifiers,
these puzzle collection covers 2 Arithmetic, 2 Crypto, 4 Graph, 8 Grid,
1 Logic, 6 Search and 7 Sequential puzzles
(Table [XIII](#A5.T13 "TABLE XIII ‣ Test-split cluster support ‣ E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).

##### Puzzle Search space

Our sampling grid varies seven factors: (1) puzzle type, (2) difficulty
bundle, (3) optimizer model, (4) worker model, (5) aggregator model, (6)
AFlow search run, and (7) MCTS iteration. Detailed information about
these factors are available in
Table [III](#A2.T3 "TABLE III ‣ Appendix B Experiment Details and Hyperparameters ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows").

1.  1.
    Puzzle type: $`p=30`$ Enigmata puzzles, e.g., Sudoku, TicTacToe,
    ZebraLogic.
2.  2.
    Difficulty bundles: *easy*/*medium*/*hard*, where 27 puzzles expose
    all three ($`b=3`$) and 3 puzzles, Hitori, LightUp, TicTacToe, only
    *medium*/*hard* ($`b=2`$). A bundle is a collection of puzzle
    instance associated with these difficulties.
3.  3.
    Optimizer model: $`o=1`$ the LLM backbone that proposes workflow
    updates in AFlow, e.g., GPT-5.4.
4.  4.
    Worker model: $`w=2`$, LLM backbones running individual task work,
    the Star-operator leaves.
5.  5.
    Aggregator model: $`g=2`$, LLM backbones handling operator-level
    synthesis.
6.  6.
    AFlow search run: $`K=5`$ AFlow searches per (puzzle, bundle, model)
    cell.
7.  7.
    AFlow search execution: $`N=20`$ MCTS rounds per AFlow search.

For each (puzzle, bundle) pair we generate $`20`$ puzzle instances
deterministically from their associated Enigmata difficulty level.

A naive grid with uniform $`b=3`$ would yield
$`30\cdot 3\cdot 1\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 5\cdot 20=36{,}000`$ workflows
from $`1{,}800`$ searches. Nonetheless, given the three puzzles missing
*easy* there are $`27\cdot 3+3\cdot 2=87`$ (puzzle, bundle) cells and
$`87\cdot 1\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 5=1{,}740`$ searches, leading to at most
$`34{,}800`$ workflows. Out of the possible $`1{,}740`$ searches,
$`1{,}701`$ completed successfully (37 mid-search aborts and 2
dispatcher misses, uniformly spread across the grid), producing
$`1{,}701\cdot 20=34{,}020`$ ($`97.7\%`$) candidate workflows.

##### Executable workflow filtering

From these $`34{,}020`$ workflows we further filter $`1{,}031`$ (3%) for
which the graphs are either missing or could not be evaluated, for
instance because a custom prompt generated by the AFlow Optimizer model
was undefined or mis-referenced.

##### Call-budget constraint

Each workflow is authorized a maximal number of atomic LLM calls of
$`20`$, given the type of puzzles, this still allows workflows that
contain multiple operators with few calls or operators that leverage
single operators with many calls. Given that each workflow is evaluated
on all the puzzles of a bundle, this leads to $`20\times 20`$ calls per
AFlow search round, and $`8{,}000`$ calls at most for a single AFlow
search.

##### Consistent Sequential Puzzle failures

After further analyses, we removed 4 of the Sequential puzzles:
EightPuzzle, NinePuzzle, FifteenPuzzle, SixteenPuzzle. Their minimal and
maximal scores remained at 0 across all searches, from further
inspection the LLM answers were either wrong attempts or simply stated
that there was no solution to the puzzles. Following this removal step
we obtain a reduced set of $`28{,}568`$ workflows.

#### B-A1 Feature-Mining Search Evolution

We conduct multiple AutoResearch runs with varying prompts, aiming at
optimizing the validation set $`R^{2}`$ while keeping the number of
features small. We considered both validation $`R^{2}`$ over the entire
population, and average $`R^{2}`$ reported across per-puzzle split.
These searches keep track of the evolution of the validation $`R^{2}`$,
features, and size of the feature set, allowing us to restore a search
step and leverage discovered feature and combination of features,
Fig. [7](#A4.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ Appendix D Analysis Phase Methodology ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
shows an example of such traces.

### B-B Analysis Phase

Each candidate design principle is evaluated per puzzle. For a given
feature, workflows are partitioned within each puzzle into a *high arm*
and a *low arm*: for binary features (e.g., presence of a SharedMemory
operator) the high arm consists of workflows where the feature is
present and the low arm those where it is absent; for count or
continuous features (e.g., mean prompt-template character length) the
partition is the per-puzzle median split, with the high arm strictly
above the median and the low arm at or below. The per-puzzle effect size
is the difference in mean score between the two arms,
$`\Delta=\mathbb{E}[\text{score}\mid\text{high arm}]-\mathbb{E}[\text{score}\mid\text{low arm}]`$,
and per-puzzle verdicts are aggregated to a principle-level verdict.

##### Predictability gate

For each puzzle, we fit a LightGBM regressor on the training-split
workflows (200 trees, learning rate 0.05, 31 leaves, min_child_samples =
10, fixed seed) predicting score from design features, and evaluate it
on the puzzle’s held-out validation workflows. A puzzle is admitted iff
validation $`R^{2}>0.05`$ *and* Spearman $`\rho>0.30`$. Both are
required: a constant predictor attains $`R^{2}=0`$ with undefined
$`\rho`$, while a rank-preserving but magnitude-compressing predictor
attains $`\rho>0`$ with $`R^{2}\leq 0`$, so the conjunction enforces
both calibration and ranking (see
§ [I](#A9 "Appendix I Gate Calibration ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).

##### Feature-set for the predictability gate

The predictability gate is parameterized by the feature set supplied to
the regression surrogate, since the admission of a puzzle is meaningful
only if the surrogate has access to features of the type the candidate
principle concerns. A puzzle whose validation $`R^{2}`$ exceeds the gate
threshold under a feature set that includes prompt-length statistics
provides no evidence that its score variation is explained by structural
design choices; conversely, restricting the surrogate to structural
features alone risks excluding puzzles whose design signal is real but
weaker than a prompt signal.

We build the feature set using both handcrafted features that leverage
the actual execution code of the workflows, associated external prompt
files, and features that were extracted during AutoResearch
explorations.

## Appendix C Design Space Specifications

We designed the operator set based on an extensive literature review
covering contemporary research papers \[[35](#bib.bib12),
[30](#bib.bib11), [15](#bib.bib25), [5](#bib.bib34), [24](#bib.bib35)\],
agentic system design whitepapers, and guidelines from popular GitHub
repositories. We cover most of the designs from \[[19](#bib.bib3)\],
with the exception of the Hybrid. Our set of operators covers commonly
used patterns; our aim was to provide the general topologies, while
leveraging AFlow ability to combine workflows, so that the core
topological components could be assembled into complex patterns while
making it possible to track operator usage.

### C-A Operator Set

The operator set is the unit of architectural variation in our search
space. Each operator is a multi-agent *topology primitive* whose call
signature exposes a small set of structural knobs (number of agents,
number of rounds, prompts) and consumes one or two of the three LLM
roles: *worker*, *aggregator* (or its role-equivalents *coordinator*,
*moderator*), and *optimizer*. The six operators currently registered
are listed below;
Fig. [2](#S2.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ Multi-Agent System Design and Topologies ‣ II Related Work ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
draws each of them for $`n=3`$ workers and $`r=2`$ rounds together with
its call and step counts, and
Fig. [3](#S4.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
shows how two operators are chained inside graph.py. All extend a common
base class that clamps the multi-agent knobs to safe ranges:
$`1\leq\texttt{num\_agents}\leq 10`$ and
$`1\leq\texttt{num\_rounds}\leq 5`$, so that any concrete workflow has a
bounded LLM-call budget regardless of the optimizer’s choices. A *round*
is one complete pass of the operator’s communication pattern (every
worker acts once); operators with $`\texttt{num\_rounds}>1`$ repeat this
pass, each time conditioned on the state produced by the previous pass.
Table [VIII](#A3.T8 "TABLE VIII ‣ C-A Operator Set ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
summarizes the parameters and call counts of each operator.

| Operator | Communication | Structure | Params | Calls |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Sequential | single agent | linear pipeline | $`r,\mathbf{p}`$ | $`|\mathbf{p}|\cdot r`$ |
| Star | isolated workers | fan-out $`\to`$ agg | $`n,\mathbf{p}_{w},p_{a}`$ | $`n+1`$ |
| SharedMemory | shared doc | writes $`\to`$ agg | $`n,r,\mathbf{p}_{w},p_{a}`$ | $`n\cdot r+1`$ |
| Debate | all-to-all | exchange $`\to`$ agg | $`n,r,\mathbf{p}_{w},p_{a}`$ | $`n\cdot r+1`$ |
| StarW/Coordinator | coord $`\leftrightarrow`$ workers | iterative hub-spoke | $`n,r,\mathbf{p}_{w},p_{a}`$ | $`(n+1)\cdot r`$ |
| DebateW/Moderator | all-to-all + mod | debate + mod/round | $`n,r,\mathbf{p}_{w},p_{a}`$ | $`(n+1)\cdot r`$ |

TABLE VIII: Composable operator primitives. $`n\in[1,10]`$ workers;
$`r\in[1,5]`$ rounds. $`\mathbf{p}_{w}`$: list of worker prompts (one
per agent); $`p_{a}`$: second-role prompt (aggregator / coordinator /
moderator). Sequential is single-agent and takes a single prompt list
$`\mathbf{p}`$. See
Fig. [2](#S2.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ Multi-Agent System Design and Topologies ‣ II Related Work ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
for the topology of each operator and
Fig. [3](#S4.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ IV Methodology: Sampling and Analysis Phases ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
for how operators compose.

##### Sequential

A pipeline of single-agent calls. The agent is invoked once per prompt
in prompts, with each call receiving the previous call’s output as
additional context, and the chain is repeated num_rounds times. There is
no multi-agent coordination: only the worker role is consumed,
$`\texttt{num\_calls}=\texttt{len(prompts)}\cdot\texttt{num\_rounds}`$.
This is the closest the operator set comes to a single-agent baseline.

##### Star

Parallel fan-out followed by a single aggregation step. num_agents
workers run in parallel on the same problem, each with its own prompt;
an aggregator then reads the concatenated worker outputs and produces a
single answer. Workers are fully isolated and never see one another’s
responses. $`\texttt{num\_calls}=\texttt{num\_agents}+1`$, mixing the
worker and aggregator roles.

##### SharedMemory

Sequential writers to a shared document, with a final aggregation pass.
On each of num_rounds rounds, the num_agents workers take turns reading
the current document and appending a contribution; the aggregator then
produces an answer from the final document. Communication is indirect
through the document state.
$`\texttt{num\_calls}=\texttt{num\_agents}\cdot\texttt{num\_rounds}+1`$.

##### Debate

All-to-all explicit communication over n_rounds rounds. Each round,
every agent revises its proposal having seen all other agents’ current
proposals; a final aggregator call collapses the last round’s proposals
into a single answer. Communication is direct, with full proposal
visibility at every step.
$`\texttt{num\_calls}=\texttt{num\_agents}\cdot\texttt{n\_rounds}+1`$.

##### StarWithCoordinator

An iterative hub-and-spoke: the coordinator participates actively across
n_rounds rounds. Each round, the coordinator broadcasts a directive, the
num_agents workers respond in parallel, and the coordinator reads all
responses to issue a revised directive; the directive after the final
round is the operator’s output. There is no worker-to-worker
communication; the aggregator role is repurposed as the coordinator.
$`\texttt{num\_calls}=(\texttt{num\_agents}+1)\cdot\texttt{n\_rounds}`$.

##### DebateWithModerator

A moderated variant of Debate: a moderator agent injects a summary or
steering prompt after every all-to-all exchange. Each agent now sees
both its peers’ proposals and the moderator’s most recent intervention
before producing its next response, and the moderator’s output on the
final round is the operator’s answer. The aggregator role is repurposed
as the moderator.
$`\texttt{num\_calls}=(\texttt{num\_agents}+1)\cdot\texttt{n\_rounds}`$,
but with a richer signal at each step than StarWithCoordinator.

### C-B Parent Selection Policy

Parent workflow selection at each AFlow expansion step follows the mixed
policy of [Zhang et al. \[33\]](#bib.bib2). Let $`s_{1},\dots,s_{n}`$
denote the scores of the top-$`k`$ previously explored candidates
($`k=4`$), with $`s_{\max}=\max_{i}s_{i}`$. The probability of selecting
candidate $`i`$ is

[TABLE]

where $`\lambda=0.2`$ controls the trade-off between uniform sampling
and score-weighted sampling, and $`\alpha=0.4`$ controls the temperature
of the score-weighted component. The shift by $`s_{\max}`$ stabilizes
the softmax against numerical overflow without altering the resulting
distribution. The uniform component prevents collapse onto the
optimizer’s prior over high-frequency operators (cf.
Table [XI](#A5.T11 "TABLE XI ‣ Test-split cluster support ‣ E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"))
and ensures broad trajectory coverage across rounds
(§ [A](#A1 "Appendix A Methodological Formalization and Statistical Estimands ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).

### C-C AFlow Integration

The AFlow codebase \[[33](#bib.bib2)\] was modified along three axes.
First, the operator registry was replaced with the six primitives of
§[C-A](#A3.SS1 "C-A Operator Set ‣ Appendix C Design Space Specifications ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"),
with corresponding updates to the optimizer-facing operator manual
injected into the modification prompt
(§[D-D](#A4.SS4 "D-D Prompts ‣ Appendix D Analysis Phase Methodology ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
Second, the dataset adapter was extended to interface with the Enigmata
generators and verifiers; this required matching Enigmata’s per-puzzle
scoring contracts to AFlow’s evaluator interface and routing the
difficulty-bundle parameter through the existing task-config plumbing.
Third, the per-round telemetry was extended to record 1) per-call
worker/aggregator role attribution, and 2) the prompts emitted by the
optimizer for each instantiation.

### C-D Enigmata Specification

Enigmata \[[3](#bib.bib1)\] bundles 36 abstract-reasoning puzzles, each
paired with a parametric generator and a deterministic, rule-based
verifier. The verifier performs an exact match against canonicalized
ground-truth output and admits no partial credit, with the per-instance
score $`\in\{0,1\}`$. We restrict our experiments to the $`30`$ puzzles
for which both generator and verifier expose programmatic interfaces;
the remaining six puzzles are excluded. Difficulty bundles are inherited
from the Enigmata partition, which was calibrated against GPT-4o pass
rates \[[3](#bib.bib1)\]: $`27`$ of the $`30`$ retained puzzles expose
the full $`\{\text{Easy},\text{Medium},\text{Hard}\}`$ bundle, while
three (Hitori, LightUp, and TicTacToe) expose only
$`\{\text{Medium},\text{Hard}\}`$.

For each (puzzle, bundle) cell, we sample $`M=20`$ instances at search
initialization and reuse this fixed set across all $`K=5`$ AFlow
searches and all workflow rounds within a search. Reusing instances
within a cell ensures that score variation across workflows reflects
workflow structure rather than instance resampling. Mixed-difficulty
bundles are left to future work. The category breakdown of the different
puzzles is reported in
Table [XIV](#A5.T14 "TABLE XIV ‣ Test-split cluster support ‣ E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows").

### C-E Filtered Puzzles and Failure Modes

Of the $`30`$ retained puzzles, four (EightPuzzle, NinePuzzle,
FifteenPuzzle, and SixteenPuzzle), all in the Sequential category, were
excluded from the analysis corpus. On these puzzles, the maximum score
across the entire set was $`0`$: no workflow ever produced a
verifier-accepted solution at any difficulty level. Inspection of
representative completions confirmed that the failure mode is uniform
across operators and difficulty bundles, with the worker model either
emitting an incorrect move sequence or asserting that no solution
exists. Because admission to the predictability gate requires
non-degenerate score variance within a puzzle, these four puzzles cannot
contribute to any per-puzzle effect-size estimate; retaining them would
inflate $`n_{\mathrm{total}}`$ without adding statistical power. The
filtered analysis corpus therefore comprises $`26`$ puzzles and
$`28{,}568`$ workflows
(Table [IX](#A5.T9 "TABLE IX ‣ E-A Statistics ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).

A secondary failure mode, applying to the executable-workflow filter
rather than to whole puzzles, removed $`1{,}031`$ workflows ($`3.0\%`$
of the post-bundle corpus) for which the AFlow Optimizer produced a
graph that could not be evaluated, typically because a custom prompt
referenced an undefined placeholder or a deleted prompt key. These
failures are uniformly distributed across the (puzzle, bundle, model)
grid and do not bias the structural feature distribution conditional on
successful execution.

### D-A Feature Engineering and Models

The feature set $`\boldsymbol{a}=\phi(W)`$ is computed only from the
workflow’s own source – the operator graph and the prompts – plus the
two allow-listed problem-side descriptors (puzzle family and difficulty
bundle). The shared operator library, while readable as a reference, is
identical across every workflow and therefore cannot produce a feature.
The base parsers cover counts and structural summaries of operator
calls, prompt-length statistics, placeholder topology, and a handful of
style markers (step-by-step, format blocks); the autonomous loop
iterates on them.

##### Train / val / test split provenance

The three-way split is assigned at the level of the AFlow *search*, not
the workflow. Each search is identified by a stable hash of its full
configuration; the assignment is deterministic per hash with a fixed
seed (so a re-run on the same configuration lands in the same split),
and the corpus-flattening step only inherits this assignment without
resampling. After flattening, every workflow lives at a content-free
identifier
$`\texttt{workflow\_id}=\text{sha1}(\texttt{search\_hash}\!:\!\texttt{round})[:16]`$;
the legacy (task, round, search_hash) path components are removed from
the directory structure, and the two task-/round-dependent imports
inside each workflow’s graph source are rewritten to neutral,
content-free forms. Together, these guarantee that the workflow source
is independent of its on-disk path. The reproducibility contract on the
loop is stronger than just split determinism: on any commit, re-running
the analysis script after the flattening step must reproduce the
committed findings snapshot and the structured metrics record
byte-for-byte. This is enforced through pinned random seeds inside every
random-state-bearing step of the regression pipeline, a frozen
dependency environment, and a prohibition on machine-local state beyond
the workflow corpus and a single targets cache.

##### Identifier exclusions

The row-level identifiers (workflow_id, round index, configuration hash)
are forbidden as features, including in any reconstructed or hashed
form. The split column itself is also forbidden.

##### Target-derived feature exclusions

No feature may depend on the primary target $`m`$ or on the workflow’s
total cost on any row. This prohibition extends to target encoding of
categoricals (smoothed or otherwise), per-group target aggregates,
residuals, ranks, and label-derived difficulty priors. A label-derived
feature is, by construction, never a property of the workflow’s design.

### D-B AutoResearch Details

Every iteration of the autonomous loop atomically commits, alongside the
analysis script, a fixed set of artifacts that together render any past
iteration replayable from the git history alone:

- •
  metrics.json: structured metrics, feature names, and top coefficients
  (the time-series source for
  Fig. [7](#A4.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ Appendix D Analysis Phase Methodology ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"));
- •
  feature_names.json: the active feature list as a flat array;
- •
  train.py: the training script driving feature engineering and
  surrogate fitting.

The fitted model and preprocessor binaries are written outside the git
tree and overwritten on each run; checking out a past commit and
re-running the analysis script regenerates them, and serves as the
byte-for-byte reproducibility check.

##### Per-commit log

A per-commit log table accompanies the artifacts and functions as the
running lab notebook of the autonomous loop. Every attempt, whether
accepted, discarded, or aborted by a runtime error, appears in this log
because the branch is append-only by construction. The verdict labels
are the agent’s own classification, recorded at the time of commit; they
are included as a reproducibility artifact rather than a primary result,
and are not used as features by the surrogate.

### D-C Caveats and Mitigated Failure Modes

The combination of an LLM-driven feature proposer and a sandboxed
evaluation loop is, by construction, susceptible to feature
constructions that exploit incidental dataset structure rather than
workflow design. Two failure modes were observed during early
AutoResearch runs and addressed before the design principles reported
were finalized.

##### Round index as a feature

An early proposal used the AFlow round index as a direct numerical
feature, exploiting the fact that later-round workflows tend to be
selected from higher-scoring parents and therefore inherit a positive
score correlation that is unrelated to architectural design. The
mitigation strips the round index from the feature-side metadata exposed
to the feature-mining loop and restricts the available artifacts to the
Python implementations of the workflows. The round index is retained in
evaluation metadata for analysis bookkeeping but is never visible to
$`\phi`$.

##### Train-mean leakage

A second early proposal computed the mean training-set score per
(puzzle, bundle) cell and added it as a feature on the validation and
test rows, yielding spuriously high $`R^{2}`$. The mitigation extends
the sandbox prompt with an explicit prohibition on aggregate statistics
derived from the target column, regardless of split.

the workflow searches, tailored to our operator set.

### E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage

The per-cell confidence intervals reported in
§[V-B](#S5.SS2 "V-B Mining and Verifying Design Principles ‣ V Empirical Analysis ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
and in
Tables [V](#A2.T5 "TABLE V ‣ B-B1 Per-Puzzle Breakdowns of Mined Principles ‣ B-B Analysis Phase ‣ Appendix B Experiment Details and Hyperparameters ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")–[VII](#A2.T7 "TABLE VII ‣ B-B1 Per-Puzzle Breakdowns of Mined Principles ‣ B-B Analysis Phase ‣ Appendix B Experiment Details and Hyperparameters ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
are computed using cluster-Wald standard errors with the AFlow search
identifier as the clustering unit. Clustering at the search level rather
than at the workflow level is the appropriate choice: workflows
generated within the same MCTS trace are not independent draws from the
workflow population, since the optimizer conditions each expansion on
the score history of its parent. The cluster-Wald estimator is
consistent in the large-cluster-count limit, with standard
recommendations requiring at least $`G\geq 15`$ clusters per arm for
nominal coverage.

##### Train-split cluster support

On the training split, per-arm cluster counts across the cells in
Tables [V](#A2.T5 "TABLE V ‣ B-B1 Per-Puzzle Breakdowns of Mined Principles ‣ B-B Analysis Phase ‣ Appendix B Experiment Details and Hyperparameters ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")–[VII](#A2.T7 "TABLE VII ‣ B-B1 Per-Puzzle Breakdowns of Mined Principles ‣ B-B Analysis Phase ‣ Appendix B Experiment Details and Hyperparameters ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
range from $`19`$ to $`47`$. A single contrast
(TicTacToe $`\times`$ op_SharedMemory_count) sits at the lower bound
with $`G=19`$ clusters in its smaller arm; all other train-side
contrasts have $`G\geq 24`$ per arm. The train-split CIs therefore lie
within the regime in which cluster-Wald inference is well-supported, and
the train-side strict-sign verdicts ($`k_{+}/k_{-}`$) are unaffected by
the issue described below.

##### Test-split cluster support

The held-out test split is, by construction, more sparsely supported at
the cluster level: the search-level split assigns each AFlow search to
exactly one of train, validation, and test, and the test split contains
$`\sim 15\%`$ of searches. Across the cells reported in the test columns
of
Tables [V](#A2.T5 "TABLE V ‣ B-B1 Per-Puzzle Breakdowns of Mined Principles ‣ B-B Analysis Phase ‣ Appendix B Experiment Details and Hyperparameters ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")–[VII](#A2.T7 "TABLE VII ‣ B-B1 Per-Puzzle Breakdowns of Mined Principles ‣ B-B Analysis Phase ‣ Appendix B Experiment Details and Hyperparameters ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"),
per-arm cluster counts range from $`4`$ to $`14`$, with the majority of
cells below $`G=10`$. The least-supported cells, both with $`G=4`$ per
arm, would fall outside the asymptotic regime.
````
