TABLE XV: Three Granularities of Mined Design Principles. We evaluate
our framework across progressively finer levels of workflow
specification: from verifying an established macro-topological failure
mode (RQ1), to comparing blackboard-style shared state against
conversational topologies (RQ2), to mining sub-topological code and
prompt template structure (RQ3).

We explored various styles of prompts and constraints for the
AutoResearch loop to mitigate overfitting, leading to different
exploration trajectories and saving protocols; we narrowed our focus to
$`300`$ feature-engineering trials spread across $`10`$ main
AutoResearch searches. We used features from these different search
traces to generate $`70`$ candidate binarized feature contrasts
(spanning the three granularities in
Table [XV](#A5.T15 "TABLE XV ‣ E-C Candidate Hypothesis Set ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")),
covering hypotheses related to prompt information, number of rounds and
agents in workflows, operator positions, and derived features combining
merging features.

For instance the two search traces from
Fig. [7](#A4.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ Appendix D Analysis Phase Methodology ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
cover two setups, one with access to both graph.py (containing the
executable workflow code) and prompt.py (custom generated prompts), and
the other with access only to graph.py. The search with access to prompt
data ran for $`49`$ trials, $`46.9\%`$ of which were accepted and grew
the feature set from 12 to 32. The search with access only to graph.py
started with an initial set of 12 features and decreased it to 9
features over 90 trials. Not all trials necessarily optimize features,
as the automated search sometimes attempts to optimize model
hyperparameters or change the model class directly.

## Appendix F Single-Backbone Baseline Performance

To contextualize the workflow-level scores,
Table [XIV](#A5.T14 "TABLE XIV ‣ Test-split cluster support ‣ E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
reports the one-shot pass rate of the three model backbones (GPT-5.4,
GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-5.4-nano) used as the worker and aggregator policies
in our experiments, evaluated directly on the per-puzzle bundle without
any multi-agent scaffolding. The same table reports the workflow-level
mean score $`\bar{\mu}_{W}`$, the workflow-level maximum score
$`\bar{\mu}_{W}^{\max}`$, and the cost in USD of the maximum-scoring
workflow.

Two patterns are noteworthy. First, on puzzles where workflows
substantially outperform the strongest single-backbone baseline, for
example, NaturalLanguageNavigation ($`0.10`$ baseline, $`0.89`$ workflow
mean) and Sudoku2 ($`0.98`$ baseline, $`0.95`$ workflow mean), the
workflow-level maximum approaches or matches the empirical ceiling,
suggesting that the AFlow search saturates these puzzles. Second, on
puzzles where all three baselines score zero (Slant, LightUp,
Minesweeper, EightPuzzle, NinePuzzle, FifteenPuzzle, SixteenPuzzle),
workflows reach at most $`0.05`$ on Slant and LightUp, while the four
sliding-tile puzzles remain at $`0.00`$ throughout and are excluded from
the analysis corpus.

## Appendix G Computational Cost Analysis

Table [X](#A5.T10 "TABLE X ‣ Test-split cluster support ‣ E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
reports the average cost in USD to evaluate one workflow against a
single puzzle instance, broken down by puzzle and difficulty. Difficulty
has a small but consistent effect on cost: the cross-puzzle mean rises
from $`\$0.0061`$ (Easy) to $`\$0.0067`$ (Hard). The 20-instance
validation bundle (one round), therefore, costs $`20\times`$ the
per-instance figure. Assuming the average cost per instance, the
evaluation of the workflows from one AFlow search is in the order
$`\$0.0064\times 20\times 20`$, as such for $`1,740`$ searches, one can
expect $`\sim\$4,454`$, to search or evaluate the workflows. The
workflow evaluation does not call the optimizer LLM, which incurs an
additional cost for the search.

## Appendix H Trace Examples

Fig. 11: AFlow search trace for a single
$`(\text{puzzle},\text{model triple})`$ cell on
EnigmataNaturalLanguageNavigation, with worker and aggregator at
gpt-5.4-nano and optimizer at gpt-5.4 (experiment_id = 1bf64a7c).
Top-left: per-round workflow score (orange bars) and best-so-far
envelope (black step line); open circles mark rounds that improved the
running maximum. Bottom-left: operator-composition trajectory, with bar
height equal to the number of operator instantiations and color denoting
operator type (gray = Sequential, purple = Star, green = Debate). Right:
MCTS lineage tree, with each node labeled by round and positioned
vertically by score. The gold path traces the root-to-best lineage
($`\text{root}\to r_{16}`$, score $`0.90`$); edge color encodes whether
the child improved (green) or regressed (red) relative to its parent.

The search trace shown in
Fig. [11](#A8.F11 "Fig. 11 ‣ Appendix H Trace Examples ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")
corresponds to a single search on a NaturalLanguageNavigation bundle
puzzle on which workflow-level performance substantially exceeds the
single-backbone baseline
(Table [XIV](#A5.T14 "TABLE XIV ‣ Test-split cluster support ‣ E-B Cluster-Robust Inference and Small-Cluster Coverage ‣ Appendix E Corpus Details and Additional Analyses ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"):
baseline $`\leq 0.15`$, workflow mean $`0.89`$).

##### Per-round and best-so-far divergence

The per-round score and the best-so-far envelope diverge substantially
throughout the search: the running maximum reaches $`0.90`$ at round
$`16`$, yet four of the final five rounds score at or below $`0.75`$.
This off-envelope variance is one motivation for our full-trace sampling
protocol: retaining all $`N=20`$ workflows from each search rather than
only the argmax preserves the design-space signal carried by the
intermediate and post-peak rounds, which an argmax-only corpus would
discard.

##### Operator-composition trajectory

The bottom-left panel shows a transition from single-operator workflows
in rounds $`1`$–$`6`$ to two-operator compositions thereafter. During
the single-operator phase, the optimizer cycles through Sequential,
Star, and Debate as the base topology; from round $`7`$ onward, the
search settles into two-operator chains and explores variants within
this richer topology class for the remainder of the trace.

##### MCTS lineage and within-search dependence

The right panel makes the dependence structure of the search explicit.
The gold path links the root to several intermediate improvements to the
peak at $`r_{16}`$, with each step on the path corresponding to a strict
score improvement (green edges); off-path explorations such as
$`r_{4}`$, $`r_{5}`$, $`r_{12}`$, and $`r_{17}`$ either regress relative
to their parent or fail to advance the running maximum.

## Appendix I Gate Calibration

Fig. 12: Per-puzzle predictability gate diagnostics across feature
subsets. For each puzzle, bars show validation $`R^{2}`$ and diamonds
show validation Spearman $`\rho`$ against the permutation-calibrated
thresholds ($`R^{2}>0.05`$ red dashed line; $`\rho>0.30`$ purple dotted
line; 95th-percentile permutation null bounds shown in gray). A puzzle
is admitted iff both metrics clear their respective thresholds on
$`D_{\text{val}}`$.

The validation thresholds $`R^{2}>0.05`$ and Spearman $`\rho>0.30`$ used
in the predictability gate
(§ [V-B](#S5.SS2 "V-B Mining and Verifying Design Principles ‣ V Empirical Analysis ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows"))
were chosen to lie a non-trivial margin above the performance attainable
by chance under the same fitting procedure. To estimate this chance
baseline, we construct a permutation null distribution: for each puzzle,
the training-split score column was shuffled ten times, the LightGBM
regressor was refit on each permuted training set, and the resulting
model was evaluated on the unshuffled validation rows. This procedure
preserves the marginal distribution of design features and the
validation targets, while severing the feature–score association that
the regressor is intended to capture; the resulting $`(R^{2},\rho)`$
pairs therefore characterize the signal that the fitting procedure
attributes to noise alone.

The 95th percentile of the pooled null distribution, computed across all
puzzles and across every feature-set variant considered during the
AutoResearch iteration loop, satisfies $`R^{2}_{p95}\leq-0.06`$ and
$`\rho_{p95}\leq 0.23`$ (visualized per puzzle in
Fig. [12](#A9.F12 "Fig. 12 ‣ Appendix I Gate Calibration ‣ Mining the Design Spaceof Multi-Agent Workflows")).
The admission thresholds therefore exceed the worst-case null upper tail
by at least $`0.07`$ on $`\rho`$ and at least $`0.11`$ on $`R^{2}`$, so
any admitted puzzle clears chance by a non-trivial and
feature-set-invariant margin. The choice is conservative in the sense
that it prioritizes false-negative robustness, admitting fewer puzzles
in exchange for stronger guarantees on those that are admitted, which is
appropriate for a downstream aggregation step in which a single floor or
zero-variance puzzle would otherwise dilute the across-puzzle contrast.

## Appendix J Broader Societal Impact

The contribution of this work is methodological rather than
capability-oriented: our framework does not introduce a new agent or
extend the capability frontier of any deployed system, but provides a
methodology under which the determinants of agentic performance can be
examined statistically. The design principles surfaced by our analysis,
although not directly deployable, contribute incrementally to the
general advance of agentic capability and inherit the dual-use risk
common to capability research.

## Appendix K LLM Usage

LLM usage is a central part of this work, as it relies on automated
workflow generation, which includes code generation. Furthermore, the
AutoResearch also conducts iterative data analysis.

We additionally use LLMs to polish the writing and check typos. LLMs
were also used for programming aid, providing initial, skeleton
implementations that were subsequently refined by the authors.
